t: 3 Popular Strategies You Should Stop Using With Difficult Students -with-difficult-students/
q: Much of your success with difficult students hinges on what you don’t do.
Any strategy that seeks to frighten or bully students into behaving will backfire every time.
Trying to convince students to behave entails telling them what they should think and how they should feel.
Picking your battles, letting misbehavior go, caving in . . . capitulation amounts to giving up on difficult students.
Holding them to a standard of behavior they need for success in school is the most compassionate thing you can do for them.
No, the secret isn’t in what you have to do. It’s in what you don’t have to do.
x: All three strategies increase the alienation and 'differentness' that difficult students already feel.

q: Routines are the lifeblood of a well-run classroom. But it’s important they’re viewed in a positive light.
A forceful or militaristic approach leads to boredom and dissatisfaction. The constant starting and stopping, the stern reminders, the hard stares and impatient body language
Many years ago, my friend Rick Morris of New Management shared with me a simple way to cultivate this spirit through music.
What’s so cool about this strategy is that the music both cues the start of the routine and sees to its conclusion.

t: 10 Simple Tweaks For Instant Behavior Improvement ovement/
q: If you’re a longtime reader of Smart Classroom Management, then you know that we hold true the belief that classroom management is knowledge based.
Before your students arrive for the day, make a decision to keep a calm demeanor throughout.
If you can cut the amount of talking you do by a third, you’ll notice a substantial difference in how well your students listen, attend, and follow your directions.
Think of the most compelling topics and activities you plan to teach that day and sell them to your students.
Relying solely on your classroom management plan frees you to enjoy being a teacher.
x: A brief, non-repetitive review of the classroom management plan keeps its importance present without belaboring it.

t: Why You Should Never Use Restrictive Methods With Difficult Students ods-with-difficult-students/
q: The tendency is to corral difficult students, to limit what they can do, where they can go, and who they can be with.
It whispers in their ear again and again that they are their misbehavior.
The truth is that difficult students need to feel like regular students before they can start behaving like regular students.
It only works if you’re consistent. It only works if you nurture and protect the relationship between you.
It is, in fact, the only surefire way to change behavior, to send them on their way after their time with you resurrected, transformed, and ready to take on the world.
x: Restricting where difficult students can go or who they can be near is a commonly used but ultimately ineffective avoidance strategy.
Linsin critiques the common tendency to corral and restrict difficult students—keeping them apart from certain peers or situations to preempt trouble.
Difficult students need the same classroom management plan and freedom-within-boundaries given to every other student, not special restrictions.

t: 4 Easy Guidelines To Calling On Students While Eliminating Rudeness, Disruptions, And Calling Out
q: The way you call on your students when they raise their hand can have a strong impact on learning and behavior.
Waiting also lowers the stress in the room. It does away with the notion that your students must compete to be heard.
They need to know that you see them and that you’re not making your decision based on who is closest, most aggressive, or within your immediate field of vision.
So unless they’re quiet and sitting down in their seats with their hand straight up in the air, you will not call upon them—ever, ever, ever.
Waiting until the moment passes before enforcing a consequence protects the flow of discussion and enables you to handle the situation gracefully and without confrontation.
x: Only calling on students following proper hand-raising etiquette eliminates aggressive hand-waving and groaning.
